title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC1LF_0RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC1LF_0RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Decided by an outside Rocq proof: it halts. Busycoq pull request 84 (Alex Havrilla of DeepMind, 2026-11-17) proves this in Rocq, and we compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch: it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions), and its transition table is this machine. It is their proof, on busycoq's definitions of a machine and of halting, and busycoq's maintainer has not yet reviewed it. Everything else on this page is what this repository found on its own, which by itself leaves the question open.

What this repository found on its own. The macro structure is identified by simulation (rounds that halve every run of equal blocks); Lean proves the shift rules the sweeps are made of and that a halt can only come from 1 1 1 D> 0. In 109 steps D read a 0 about 21,000 times and every time the left neighbours were 1 1 0 or blank, one cell short of a halt.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,990 cells have been visited and 26,870 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.113). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.519).

claims.title: The sweeps' shift rules
claims.text: Moving right, A (with 1 0 behind it) and C (with 1 behind it) turn each pair 11 into 01, 6 steps a pair: a run of 2n ones becomes (01)n. Moving left, C (facing a 0) and D (facing a 1) turn each 01 back into 11, 2 steps a pair. B runs over 1s. Each holds for every n and every surrounding tape.

claims.title: The shape of a halt
claims.text: From 1 1 1 D> 0 the machine reaches F on a 1 in 3 steps and halts on the next. Conversely (by reading the table, not formalized) F is entered only from E on a 1, E only from A on a 1, and A has a 1 to its left only when it came from D on a 0 (from C or F it has a 0 there), so every halt comes this way.

claims.title: Near misses: D reads a 0 next to exactly two 1s
claims.text: In the first 109 steps D reads a 0 21,121 times with 1 1 0 to its left (one 1 short of a halt) and 181 times at the blank left end; never with three 1s.

claims.title: Rounds and the halving law
claims.text: Sample the run when the head is in A at the left end of the tape (rounds; consecutive samples about 1.25 times further apart). At every sample the tape is a list of blocks 1k 00, almost all with k = 6j+1 and grouped in long runs of equal blocks, lowest level at the right. Between consecutive rounds a run of n blocks of level j becomes a run of ⌊n/2⌋−1 to ⌈n/2⌉+1 blocks of level j+1 (checked for every run of at least 10 blocks after the first 1.2·107 steps, to 1.6·109), and a new run of level-0 blocks 100 appears, alternately large and small (the large ones growing by about 1.25 each time: 1590, 2086, 2664, 3330, 4130, 5171). A few odd blocks (k = 5, 11, 17, ...) sit between the runs.

claims.title: Same tapes as its twin
claims.text: At all 190 left-end samples in the first 2·109 steps the tape is exactly that of 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC--- (the step counts differ slightly, by 0.005 %); the two tables do the same thing with different states on the short path through A or E. The sibling 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC0LF_0RB--- has the same blocks and the same rules but different counts.

claims.title: Within a round: an expanding bouncer
claims.text: After the left-end sample the head runs right to a point well inside the tape and then zig-zags in a window whose left edge creeps left and right edge creeps right (by a few cells per bounce, using the halving and doubling rules above), until the window reaches the left end: the next sample. This is where the square-root growth on the right comes from.
claims.where: as for the sibling 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC0LF_0RB---, same rules

claims.title: No closed tape language from short windows
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with windows of K = 3 and 6 cells finds a closed set, but every one allows a halt (24 to 480 halting abstract configurations); n-gram CPS (widths 3 to 7, with history and LRU) also fails.
claims.where: tools/py/bbtools/ctl.py; tools/c/ngramcps.c (run for the G02 group, not stored here)

claims.title: No halt in the first 5.86×10<sup>13</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 5.86×1013 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.00×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 3,618 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It halts exactly if D ever reads a 0 with three 1s on its left. That needs one of the odd blocks or a run boundary to line up badly during a round; the halving law looks like a binary counter on the run lengths with carries (the odd blocks), and nothing in the run so far approaches it. A proof would need the exact round map, including what happens to odd counts and to the junk between runs.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LC_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_0RA1RF_0LC--- up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each. The same tapes at another pace, whatever the states, as 2 other holdouts (listed on the explainer page).

check: gcc -O2 -o samples holdouts/1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC1LF_0RA---/c/samples.c && ./samples 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC1LF_0RA--- 2000000000 A L 0 100000 > left.txt && python3 holdouts/1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RA_1LA1LC_0LC1LF_0RA---/py/rounds.py left.txt

explainer.lede: It halts. The tape is a list of blocks of 1s whose lengths go up in steps of 6; every round halves each run of equal blocks, moves it up one length and adds a fresh run of short blocks. After about 10<sup>361</sup> steps the leftovers of this halving set up the one pattern that stops it: busycoq pull request 84 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind proves it in Rocq.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 36,990 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Each round, every run of equal blocks halves and moves up a level.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 1.00×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: A counter of digit rows, run by a proved engine
html: The proof is busycoq pull request 84 by Alex Havrilla of DeepMind. We compiled it here with Coq 8.20.1 on busycoq's BB6 branch in about 87 seconds; it uses no axioms (Print Assumptions halt prints “Closed under the global context”). It does not find a formula for the run. It builds a fast simulator, the engine, proves in Coq that every step of the engine is a true statement about the machine, and then lets the engine run the machine from the blank tape until it halts. This file (4,750 lines) has its own version of the engine, written directly for this machine, and keeps the newest row of digits D 0 as a separate counter.

A known table. No reflection is needed. Renaming this machine's A, B, C, D as D, A, B, C gives the table 1RB1RA_1LC0RD_1LD1LB_1RA0LE_0LB1LF_0RD--- started in state D, and the proof's rules are those of that table written with this machine's state names. The same table started in state B, with the tape reflected, is 1RB0LC_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_0RA1RF_0LC---, proved halting by busycoq pull request 82.

Digits and three moments. Write wn for the word w written n times. The proof's main word is the digit D n = 1 (11)n 00: a run of 2n+1 ones followed by two blanks. Call n its level. The blocks of 1, 7, 13, 19, … ones of the sections below (their levels 0, 1, 2, 3) are the digits D 0, D 3, D 6, D 9. Most of the tape is a long sequence of digits, mostly in rows of equal ones, the highest levels towards the left and the lowest at the right end. Near the left end, where the head turns, lie a few other kinds of word, among them blocks (10)b and (111)k. The proof watches the head at three kinds of moment: CfgR, state B at the word 0100, heading right over the digits; CfgL, state C heading left with a 1 just behind it; and CfgJ, state D heading left with 100 just behind it and a +1 to deliver.

Macro rules. About twenty rules say how the machine gets from one such moment to the next, for every level and every surrounding tape. Heading right, the head turns each digit D n it crosses into S n = 1 (01)n+1, a word of the same length. Heading left in CfgL it turns S n back into D n; in CfgJ it turns it into D (n+1), which is how a +1 is delivered. At the blank end of the tape the head writes two new digits D 0 and turns back. On the left, each 111 of a block (111)k is used up by one turn, so the block is a timer that allows k more round trips. And a round trip that finds two digits D 0 side by side merges them: 10 D0 D0 becomes D2 10, and the digit before them gets a +1; over a row, 2k digits D 0 become about k digits D 3. Rows of higher digits are merged in pairs in the same way, through a longer detour over the left part.

A counter. Together these rules make the digits a counter. Its places are the levels 0, 3, 6, …, and the number of digits in a row is the value at that place. Each pass halves a row and carries it one place up, while fresh digits D 0 keep arriving at the right end. This is binary counting with rows instead of bits, so a row of n digits lasts about log2 n passes. The halving is not exact: a row with an odd count leaves a digit over, and the proof has rules for these leftovers (it calls them defects). Where the leftovers end up depends on the parities of huge counts, and no formula for them is known. That is why the community calls such a machine a chaotic Bell.

The engine. The engine is a program written in Coq. It stores the tape compactly: the left part as a list of words with repeat counts, the digits as a list of pairs (level, how many in a row), all numbers in binary. In one engine step it looks at the tape near the head, picks the rule that applies, often a whole batch of them (k round trips at once, with k found by a division), and writes down the result. Where no rule fits, it makes single machine steps. One theorem, proved for every possible compact tape, says that each engine step is correct: the machine really goes from the tape before to the tape after, and when the engine reports a halt, the machine really halts.

How it stops. It halts only when state D reads a 0 with three 1s to its left, which leads to F on a 1; the proof's last rule recognises this pattern. Before the proof, the run had come one cell short of this about 21,000 times (see below). Nothing in the proof predicts when the leftovers will set this up; the engine simply runs until they do. Coq's virtual machine (vm_compute) evaluates the engine from the blank tape for exactly 1,240,545 steps and finds the halting pattern at the end, when the newest row holds about 10181 digits D 0; by the proof's estimate the machine itself has then run about 10361 steps. So the computer checks one long but finite computation. What holds for all sizes (the rules, the batches, the correctness of every engine step) is proved by symbolic reasoning in Coq.

sections.eyebrow: What the tape is made of
sections.heading: Runs of equal blocks
html: Watch the run only at the moments the head stands in state A at the left end of the tape. At every such moment the tape is a list of blocks 1k 00 (k ones, then two zeros), and almost every k has the form 6j+1: 1, 7, 13, 19, 25, ... Call j the block's level. Equal blocks come in long runs. Here is the tape at step 1,032,996,043, each block written as its k, x meaning repetition (so 7x570 is 570 copies of 1700):

The highest levels are on the left, the lowest on the right; the whole tape is 37,755 cells wide. The left part grows only like the logarithm of the time (a new level now and then), the right part like its square root.

sections.heading: Every run halves
html: The next sample, at step 1,315,832,564, reads:

Compare: the 890 blocks of level 0 became 445 blocks of level 1, the 2065 of level 1 became 1032 of level 2, 176 → 87, 415 → 207, 33 → 16, 82 → 41, 16 → 7. Every run halved and went up a level, and a fresh run of 5171 level-0 blocks appeared on the right. That is the law at every round we checked: n blocks of level j become between ⌊n/2⌋−1 and ⌈n/2⌉+1 blocks of level j+1. So a run born with n blocks survives about log2 n rounds, which is why the number of levels, and the left part of the tape, grows only logarithmically.

How the halving is done: a round is an expanding bouncer. The head runs right into the tape and then zig-zags in a window that widens on both sides a few cells per trip. Going right, it rewrites pairs of ones 11 as 01; going left it rewrites 01 back as 11 (these shift rules are proved in Lean). Doing so it eats one block of a pair and grows the other by six ones.

sections.heading: One cell short, twenty thousand times, and then not
html: The machine has one halting transition (F reading a 1), and following the table backwards there is only one way into it: D reads a 0 while the three cells to its left are 1. Lean checks that 1 1 1 D> 0 halts four steps later. In the first 109 steps D read a 0 about 21,000 times, and every single time the cells to its left were 1 1 0: the block to its left had exactly two ones. So whether the machine halts is whether some round ever brings D to a 0 next to a longer run of ones, for instance through one of the odd blocks (5, 11, 17, ...) left over when a run has an odd count.

Before the proof nothing more was known. The run looks like a binary counter on the lengths of the runs, with the odd leftovers as carries, and short-window invariants (CTL up to 6 cells, n-gram CPS up to width 7) did not decide it. They could not: the machine does halt. The proved engine of busycoq pull request 84 finds D on a 0 next to three 1s after 1,240,545 engine steps, about 10361 machine steps (see How the proof works).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.113). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.519).
After 109 steps the tape spans 36,990 cells (497 left of the start, 28,611 right), with a density of 1s of 0.726.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0LC_1RC1RA_1LD0RE_1LA1LD_0RA1RF_0LC---: rename A→C, B→D, C→A, D→B, E→E, F→F and exchange left and right; it is this table started in state C, in a mirror

Same tapes at another pace (observed, not proved). Leave the states aside and compare only the tape and the place of the head. Then a large part of the first 107 configurations of this machine are configurations of the machines below, in the same order and up to the end of the run. The steps at which they occur differ, the tables are not renamings of each other, and equal tapes with different states may be continued differently, so this does not tie the halting questions together.

  • 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC---: 9,995,929 configurations, the last at step 10,000,000 here and step 9,995,928 there
  • 1RB0RF_0LC---_1LD1LC_1RE0LA_1RA1RD_0RD0RF (in a mirror): 8,003,899 configurations, the last at step 8,007,428 here and step 9,999,998 there

summary: A cascade of halving runs: the tape is runs of equal blocks 1^(6j+1) 00, and each round an expanding zig-zag sweep turns a run of n blocks of level j into about n/2 blocks of level j+1 and lays down a fresh run of level 0. Same tapes as 1RB0LE_1RC1RB_1LD0RE_1LA1LC_1RB0LF_0LC---. Decided outside: busycoq PR 84 proves in Rocq that it halts (compiled here).
